title: Show Your Work! 10 Ways to Share Your Creativity and Get Discovered
author: Austin Kleon
summary:
Show Your Work! is Austin Kleon's follow-up to his earlier book Steal Like an Artist, and it addresses a specific problem the first book left open: once you've learned how to find inspiration and generate creative work by building on what came before, how do you actually get that work seen by anyone? Kleon's answer runs directly against the old model of the reclusive genius who works in isolation and unveils a finished masterpiece to the world — he argues that in a networked, always-online era, the process of sharing your work in progress, openly and generously, is itself one of the most powerful ways to build an audience, get discovered, and improve as a creative practitioner.

The book is structured as ten short, punchy chapters, each built around one specific principle for sharing creative work without feeling like you're either shamelessly self-promoting or paralyzed by perfectionism. Kleon opens with the idea that you don't need to be a genius to have something worth sharing — you just need to think of yourself as an amateur, in the original sense of someone who does something for the love of it, which frees you from the pressure of only sharing polished, expert-level output. He builds from there into the idea of thinking process, not product — documenting the everyday steps, materials, and decisions behind your work, which is both more honest and more interesting to an audience than only ever showing finished results.

The middle chapters cover practical territory: sharing something small every day rather than waiting for a big reveal, opening up your cabinet of curiosities (the influences and inspirations that feed your work) to build genuine connection with your audience, telling the story behind your work clearly since a good story travels further than the work alone, and teaching what you know as a way of building both mastery and community simultaneously. Kleon is consistently pragmatic about the discomfort many creative people feel around self-promotion, reframing "sharing" as distinct from "showing off" and arguing that generosity, not salesmanship, is the actual engine that makes sharing work sustainably.

The closing chapters address the harder, less glamorous realities of a sustained public creative practice: handling criticism without being derailed by it, learning to sell without feeling like you're selling out, and — perhaps the book's most quietly important closing message — knowing when to step away, go quiet, and protect the parts of your creative life and process that don't need to be shared at all. The book closes by reiterating that sharing your work is a long, cumulative practice rather than a single moment of self-promotion, and that showing up consistently, generously, and honestly over time is what actually builds a durable creative career and audience.

sections.title: You Don't Have to Be a Genius
sections.summary:
This opening chapter dismantles the "lone genius" myth of creative work, arguing that the pressure to only share work once you've achieved mastery keeps far too many people from ever sharing anything at all. Kleon introduces the idea of thinking of yourself as an amateur — in the literal sense of someone who does something for love, not necessarily expertise — as a way to lower the psychological barrier to sharing.

He uses examples of well-known creative figures who built audiences and skill simultaneously by sharing amateur-level work publicly and improving in view of others, rather than waiting for private mastery before ever going public, arguing this visibility actually accelerates growth rather than exposing weakness.

The chapter closes by reframing "having something worth sharing" as a much lower bar than most creative people assume, setting up the next chapter's argument for sharing process rather than only finished product.
keyLessons: Reframe "amateur" as someone who works out of love, not as an insult implying low skill.
Recognize that sharing work publicly before you feel expert-level ready can accelerate skill growth, not expose weakness.
Lower your personal bar for "worth sharing" — the bar most creative people set for themselves is unnecessarily high.

sections.title: Think Process, Not Product
sections.summary:
This chapter argues that documenting and sharing the process behind creative work — the messy steps, materials, decisions, and false starts — is both more honest and more genuinely interesting to an audience than only ever revealing polished final products.

Kleon covers practical ways to document process (photos of works in progress, notes on decisions and dead ends, behind-the-scenes glimpses) and argues this practice serves two purposes at once: it builds a more engaged, invested audience who feels like insiders, and it creates a kind of public record that helps the creator themselves reflect on and improve their own process over time.

The chapter closes by connecting process-sharing to authenticity — audiences increasingly value seeing how something was made, not just what was made — which sets up the next chapter's specific guidance on sharing daily rather than only at major milestones.
keyLessons: Document and share the messy middle of your process, not only finished, polished outcomes.
Treat process documentation as a tool for your own reflection and improvement, not just audience content.
Recognize that audiences increasingly value transparency about how work was made, not only the final result.

sections.title: Share Something Small Every Day
sections.summary:
This chapter makes the case for a daily, incremental sharing habit — a "daily dispatch" — over the old model of working in isolation for a long stretch and then unveiling a single, big reveal. Kleon argues small, consistent sharing builds audience relationships gradually and reduces the pressure and risk associated with any single share.

He works through practical formats for small daily shares (a single image, a short note, a small work-in-progress update) and argues this rhythm keeps a creative practice visible and alive in an audience's attention without requiring a major, high-stakes launch moment every time.

The chapter closes by connecting daily sharing to the compounding nature of an audience-building practice — small, consistent actions accumulate into a substantial body of shared work and a real audience relationship over time, which the following chapter builds on with guidance on sharing influences specifically.
keyLessons: Build a habit of sharing something small and low-stakes regularly, rather than saving everything for one big reveal.
Use simple, low-effort formats (a single image, a short note) to keep a daily sharing habit sustainable.
Treat audience-building as a compounding practice — small consistent shares accumulate into real relationships over time.

sections.title: Open Up Your Cabinet of Curiosities
sections.summary:
This chapter encourages creators to share not just their own finished work but the influences, references, and inspirations that feed it — Kleon's "cabinet of curiosities" metaphor for the mix of things a creative person collects and draws from.

He argues that sharing your influences openly does double duty: it's generous and genuinely interesting content for an audience in its own right, and it builds real connection and community with people who share those same interests, rather than only positioning you as a solitary output-generating machine.

The chapter closes by connecting curiosity-sharing to community-building specifically, arguing that an audience built around shared interests and generosity is more durable than one built purely around admiration for finished output — setting up the next chapter's focus on storytelling.
keyLessons: Share your influences and inspirations openly, not just your finished output.
Treat sharing your interests as genuine content in its own right, not just supplementary context.
Build community around shared curiosity and generosity, which tends to be more durable than admiration alone.

sections.title: Tell Good Stories
sections.summary:
This chapter argues that a well-told story about your work travels further, and often matters more to how it's received, than the technical quality of the work alone — and covers practical guidance on how to tell the story behind creative work clearly and honestly.

Kleon works through basic storytelling structure applied to creative work-sharing (what problem were you solving, what was hard about it, what did you learn) and cautions against either over-hyping a story dishonestly or under-explaining it so thoroughly that an audience has no way in.

The chapter closes by connecting good storytelling to the earlier process-sharing chapter — the story of your work and the process behind it are deeply related, and both serve the same underlying goal of making your work more accessible and human to an audience, setting up the next chapter's focus on teaching.
keyLessons: Tell the honest story behind your work — the problem, the difficulty, the learning — not just the finished result.
Avoid both dishonest over-hyping and under-explaining your work to the point an audience has no way in.
Treat storytelling and process-sharing as connected practices serving the same goal of accessibility.

sections.title: Teach What You Know
sections.summary:
This chapter argues that teaching what you've learned — even as a relative beginner — is one of the most effective ways to both deepen your own mastery and build a genuinely engaged audience simultaneously.

Kleon covers the idea that you don't need to be the world's leading expert to teach something useful; teaching what you learned yesterday to someone one step behind you is both valuable to them and clarifying for your own understanding, since explaining something forces genuine comprehension.

The chapter closes by framing teaching as a form of generosity that pays back to the teacher as much as the audience, reinforcing the book's recurring theme that sharing generously, rather than strategically withholding knowledge as a competitive advantage, is the more sustainable long-term practice — setting up the following chapters' more defensive guidance on handling the downsides of visibility.
keyLessons: Teach what you learned recently, even as a relative beginner — it's valuable to others and clarifying for yourself.
Recognize teaching as a generosity practice that builds your own mastery, not just your audience's knowledge.
Resist strategically withholding knowledge as competitive advantage; generous sharing tends to be more sustainable.

sections.title: Don't Turn Into Human Spam
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the discomfort many creative people feel about self-promotion directly, drawing a clear line between sharing generously (which builds real relationships) and "human spam" — self-promotion that only pushes outward without offering genuine value or engaging with others.

Kleon offers practical guidance for staying on the right side of that line: engaging authentically with other people's work, not just broadcasting your own; sharing things because they're genuinely interesting or useful, not purely as a promotional vehicle; and being mindful of the difference between building a relationship with an audience and simply extracting attention from one.

The chapter closes by reframing the goal of sharing work as building real, reciprocal relationships over time, not maximizing short-term attention, setting up the next chapter's guidance on handling the inevitable criticism that comes with sustained visibility.
keyLessons: Distinguish sharing that builds real relationships from "human spam" that only broadcasts outward.
Engage genuinely with other people's work as part of your sharing practice, not only your own output.
Prioritize reciprocal relationship-building over maximizing short-term attention.

sections.title: Learn to Take a Punch
sections.summary:
This chapter prepares readers for the harder realities of sustained public creative sharing — criticism, negative feedback, and the emotional toll of visibility — arguing that learning to absorb criticism without being derailed by it is a necessary skill for anyone sharing work consistently over time.

Kleon covers practical approaches to handling criticism: distinguishing genuinely useful feedback from noise, not overreacting to any single critical response, and maintaining enough separation between your identity and your work that criticism of the work doesn't have to feel like an attack on you personally.

The chapter closes by normalizing criticism as an inevitable and even useful part of a sustained public creative practice rather than a sign that sharing was a mistake, setting up the following chapter's related guidance on selling your work without feeling compromised by it.
keyLessons: Distinguish genuinely useful criticism from noise, and don't let any single critical response derail your practice.
Maintain separation between your identity and your work so criticism of the work doesn't feel like a personal attack.
Treat criticism as a normal, expected part of sustained public sharing, not evidence that sharing was a mistake.

sections.title: Sell Out
sections.summary:
This chapter tackles the discomfort many creative people feel around monetizing their work, reframing "selling" as a natural and legitimate extension of sharing generously over time, rather than a betrayal of creative integrity.

Kleon argues that an audience built through genuine, generous sharing over time is far more receptive to eventually paying for related work or products than an audience approached purely transactionally from the start, and that avoiding selling entirely, out of fear of "selling out," often just means failing to sustain a creative practice financially at all.

The chapter closes by framing selling as simply the natural extension of a trust relationship built through consistent, generous sharing, setting up the book's final chapter on knowing when and how to step back from public sharing.
keyLessons: Recognize that an audience built through generous sharing is more receptive to eventually paying for your work.
Treat "selling out" fears as often actually fear of the vulnerability of asking to be paid, not a real ethical line.
View selling as the natural extension of trust built through consistent, generous sharing, not a betrayal of it.

sections.title: Stick Around
sections.summary:
This closing chapter shifts from the how of sharing to the when — and specifically, the when-not-to — arguing that a sustainable creative-sharing practice requires knowing when to go quiet, protect unshared parts of your process, and step back from public visibility without treating that step-back as failure.

Kleon reinforces that sharing your work is a long, cumulative practice built over years, not a single moment of self-promotion, and that the creators who benefit most from sharing are the ones who stick around consistently over the long term rather than burning out through relentless, undifferentiated visibility.

The book closes by returning to its founding argument: showing your work, done generously and sustainably over time, builds both a genuine audience and a genuinely improving creative practice — but only if the sharer protects their own capacity to keep doing it for the long haul.
keyLessons: Protect some parts of your process and creative life as unshared, without treating that boundary as a failure of openness.
Treat sustained, long-term consistency as more valuable than intense, short-term bursts of visibility.
Remember that the goal is a durable creative practice, not maximum visibility at any single moment.
Lower your personal bar for "worth sharing" — thinking of yourself as an amateur who works for love removes unnecessary pressure.
Document and share your process, not just finished output, since it's more honest and more engaging to an audience.
Build a habit of sharing something small regularly rather than saving everything for one big reveal.
Share your influences and interests openly as genuine content, not just context for your own output.
Tell the honest story behind your work — the problem, the difficulty, the learning — to make it more accessible.
Teach what you've recently learned, even as a beginner, since it clarifies your own understanding and helps others.
Distinguish generous sharing that builds relationships from "human spam" that only broadcasts outward.
Maintain enough separation between your identity and your work that criticism doesn't feel like a personal attack.

quotes.text: Nobody cares about your resume, because nobody's going to read it. What they care about is what you can do, and demonstrating what you can do is far more powerful than a list of credentials.
The amateur is not afraid to be wrong, to look silly, to play.
Share what you love, and the people who love the same things will find you.
The way to get an audience to care about you is to care about them first.

whoThisIsFor: Creative practitioners — writers, artists, makers, and professionals doing any kind of visible creative work — who have something worth sharing but feel blocked by perfectionism or discomfort with self-promotion.
whenToReadThis: Read it when you have a body of creative work sitting privately unfinished or unshared, and self-promotion anxiety is the main thing standing between you and an audience.

authorBio.name: Austin Kleon
authorBio.bio:
Austin Kleon is an American writer and artist known for a body of work that blends visual art, writing, and practical creative advice, most notably through his bestselling Steal Like an Artist, which established his signature short, illustrated, highly quotable style of creative-practice guidance.

Kleon's own creative practice — including his well-known "newspaper blackout poetry," created by redacting newspaper text to reveal new poems — has served as a recurring example across his books of the process-over-product, share-generously philosophy he advocates, giving his advice a grounded, practiced quality rather than purely theoretical guidance.

Show Your Work! extended his Steal Like an Artist framework specifically into the question of audience-building and visibility, cementing Kleon's reputation as a widely read voice on sustainable creative practice in the social-media era, alongside his ongoing newsletter and public speaking work on similar themes.
notableWorks: Keep Going: 10 Ways to Stay Creative in Good Times and Bad

conceptsFrameworks.name: Think Process, Not Product
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Kleon's core recommendation to document and share the everyday steps, decisions, and materials behind creative work, rather than only ever revealing polished final results — treated as both more honest and more engaging to build audience connection.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Cabinet of Curiosities
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Kleon's metaphor for the mix of influences, references, and inspirations a creative person collects and draws from, and his argument that sharing this collection openly builds genuine community and connection beyond admiration for finished work alone.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Open Up Your Cabinet of Curiosities

conceptsFrameworks.name: Human Spam
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Kleon's term for self-promotion that only broadcasts outward without offering genuine value or engaging with others, used to draw a clear line between generous sharing (which builds relationships) and purely extractive self-promotion.

actionSteps: Share one piece of your current work-in-progress today — a photo, a note, a small update — rather than waiting until it's finished.
Write a short, honest account of the problem and difficulty behind your most recent finished piece of work, and share it alongside the work itself.
Teach one thing you learned in the past month to someone one step behind you, in writing or conversation.
Identify one recurring critical response to your work and separate what's genuinely useful feedback from what's just noise, in writing.
Deliberately protect one part of your current creative process as unshared this month, and notice whether that boundary changes how sustainable sharing the rest feels.
reflectionQuestions: What's the actual bar you've set for "worth sharing," and where did that bar come from?
Where has fear of "selling out" quietly stopped you from asking to be paid for work an audience already values?

points: The book's advice is oriented heavily around online, platform-based visibility (social media, blogs), and its specific tactical guidance has aged unevenly as the platforms it references have changed significantly since publication, even though the underlying principles remain broadly applicable.

Kleon's own success sharing process and influences built partly on his prior book's success and an existing audience; readers starting from zero audience may find the "share small daily updates and get discovered" path considerably slower and less reliable in practice than the book's brisk, encouraging tone suggests.

The book gives relatively light treatment to the real risks of consistent public sharing for people in more vulnerable circumstances (marginalized creators facing disproportionate harassment, people in contexts where visibility carries professional or personal risk), treating the "don't turn into human spam" and "learn to take a punch" chapters as sufficient coverage of the downsides of visibility for all readers alike.

As a short, aphoristic, highly illustrated book, it prioritizes accessible principles over deep, evidence-based exploration of audience-building or platform algorithm mechanics, which some readers looking for a more rigorous marketing or growth strategy resource may find too light.
criticalTake.contextNote: Published in 2014, several of the book's platform-specific references have dated, though its underlying argument about generous, process-focused sharing as a sustainable creative practice has remained broadly relevant as the specific platforms have shifted.

sourceNotes: Synthesis is based on strong general knowledge of Kleon's well-documented ten-chapter structure and core concepts (amateurism, process over product, the cabinet of curiosities, human spam, teaching, criticism, and selling), which are consistently and extensively documented across publisher materials and widely available book summaries; quotes were selected from commonly cited, consistently reproduced lines associated with the book. No significant informational gaps were encountered for this well-documented, mainstream bestselling title.
